ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: In the circuit shown in Figure 14, after switch S is closed, the two bulbs $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ both emit light normally. Later, due to some fault, $L_{2}$ suddenly becomes brighter and the voltmeter reading decreases. From this, what may the fault be?
ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_answer: The capacitor is broken down and short-circuited
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, the power supply is marked E, internal resistance r, and there is a switch S at the bottom. The external circuit on the left side has three parallel branches from the left bus to the middle node: the upper branch is capacitor C, the middle branch is bulb L1, and the lower branch is resistor R1. From the middle node to the right bus there are two parallel branches: the upper branch is resistor R2, and the lower branch is bulb L2. Voltmeter V is connected between the left and right buses, measuring the voltage across the two ends of the external circuit, that is, the terminal voltage of the power supply. Reasoning: After the switch is closed and has worked stably for a period of time, in the DC steady state capacitor C is equivalent to an open circuit, so the original external circuit can be regarded as the equivalent branch where the left section L1 and R1 are located in series with the parallel part of the right section R2 and L2, and L2 only obtains a part of the voltage on the right section. The problem says that after the fault L2 suddenly becomes brighter, indicating that the voltage across L2 increases; at the same time the voltmeter reading decreases, indicating that the terminal voltage of the power supply decreases, which usually corresponds to the equivalent resistance of the external circuit decreasing and the total current increasing, making the voltage drop Ir on the internal resistance r increase. If capacitor C is broken down and short-circuited, then the left section is short-circuited, and the equivalent resistance of the left section where L1 and R1 are located becomes approximately 0; the parallel part of the right section R2 and L2 is then directly connected to the terminal voltage of the power supply, and the voltage across L2 is greater than when it was originally divided in series, so L2 becomes brighter; at the same time, the total resistance of the external circuit decreases, the total current increases, the voltage division on the internal resistance increases, and the terminal voltage, that is, the voltmeter reading, decreases. Both phenomena are consistent. Final answer: Capacitor C is broken down and short-circuited.
